soil-chem-154.title: Colloids, particles too small to settle quietly
soil-chem-154.text: The most active particles in soil are less than 1 μm across. Mixed into water, particles this small form a colloid: a mixture in which microscopically small insoluble particles are dispersed through another substance. The suspended particles are the dispersed phase; the medium around them is the continuous phase. IUPAC puts colloidal particles roughly between 1 nanometer and 1 micrometer in at least one dimension, and says those limits are not rigid. Some colloids look translucent because their particles scatter light, the Tyndall effect. The particles push and pull through several forces, from electrostatic attraction or repulsion to always-present, short-range van der Waals attraction. In soil, the colloidal fraction is tiny particles of {{ref:soil-found-040}} and {{ref:soil-bio-089}} whose positive or negative charges vary with soil pH. Francesco Selmi began the study of colloids in 1845, and Thomas Graham coined the word in 1861.

soil-chem-160.title: Zeta potential, the voltage that keeps particles apart
soil-chem-160.text: A colloid's fate can hang on a few tens of millivolts. As a particle moves through liquid, a thin film of fluid travels with it. The boundary where that film ends and the still fluid begins is the slipping plane. The electrical potential there is the zeta potential, written ζ and usually given in millivolts. It is not the same as the potential at the particle's surface, but it is often the only way to characterize the charged layers around a {{ref:soil-chem-154}}. It is also a handy gauge of stability. Magnitudes of 0 to 5 mV give rapid coagulation, 30 to 40 mV moderate stability, 40 to 60 mV good stability and over 61 mV excellent stability. To measure it, an electric field is applied. Particles drift toward the opposite electrode at a velocity proportional to their zeta potential, tracked by laser Doppler anemometry. Where pH–zeta potential curves cross titration curves lies the {{ref:soil-chem-075}}.

soil-chem-155.title: Colloidal stability: why some suspensions never clear
soil-chem-155.text: Whether a cloudy suspension stays cloudy comes down to a contest of forces. Colloidal stability is the ability of particles to stay suspended instead of clumping. A {{ref:soil-chem-154}} stays stable while the attraction between particles is below kT, the energy of thermal motion. Above that, they begin to clump: aggregation, flocculation or coagulation. Coagulation may mean permanent clumping, flocculation a reversible kind that forms a floc. The clumps settle out or cream to the top, ending the suspension. Particles are held apart electrostatically, by the like charges of their surrounding layers of counterions, or sterically, by adsorbed polymer or surfactant layers. Adding salt shrinks the charged layer, and shifting pH neutralizes surface charge. Either removes the repulsion and lets van der Waals forces win. When {{ref:soil-chem-160}} falls below about ±5 mV, rapid coagulation tends to follow. Charged polymers can also bridge particles: negatively charged clay flocculates when a positively charged polymer is added.

soil-chem-158.title: Particle aggregation: how suspended grains clump and fall
soil-chem-158.text:
A stable suspension can be undone by a pinch of the right salt. Particle aggregation is the sticking together of dispersed particles into irregular flocs or agglomerates, which destabilizes a {{ref:soil-chem-154}}. It also goes by coagulation or flocculation. Salts or chemicals called coagulants or flocculants trigger it, and it can be reversible or irreversible. Growing agglomerates settle out as sediment. In concentrated suspensions they link instead into a colloidal gel. The reverse, {{ref:soil-chem-161}}, hardly happens on its own, though stirring or shear can drive it.

Salt works by screening the repulsion of the charged layers around each particle, so van der Waals attraction dominates. Chemists track this with the stability ratio W. It is near one in fast aggregation and very large in a stable suspension. Each counter-ion charge has a critical coagulation concentration. Because particles are often negative, multivalent metal cations are highly effective coagulants. Polymers cut both ways. They can protect particles by steric repulsion, or, when loosely adsorbed, bridge two particles in bridging flocculation.

The way particles meet matters too. Aggregation driven only by diffusion is perikinetic; aggregation sped up by shear, such as stirring, is orthokinetic. The clusters are mass fractals, shapes whose density changes with size. Fast, diffusion-limited aggregation builds loose clusters (d ≈ 1.8), and slow, reaction-limited aggregation compact ones (d ≈ 2.1). These outcomes follow from the balance described in {{ref:soil-chem-155}}.

soil-chem-157.title: DLVO theory: attraction, repulsion and the barrier between
soil-chem-157.text: Two charged particles in a liquid feel a pull and a push at once. DLVO theory adds them up. It sums van der Waals attraction and electrical double-layer repulsion to give a quantitative account of {{ref:soil-chem-155}}. Both forces grow as particles approach, and their sum traces a curve. A deep primary minimum lies at very close range, an energy barrier further out, and a shallow secondary minimum beyond it. The barrier's height shows how stable the dispersion is; if it does not exceed the thermal energy, particles aggregate. Particles trapped in the primary minimum coagulate for good, while those in the secondary minimum are held weakly and easily redispersed. Derjaguin and Landau proposed the theory in 1941, and Verwey and Overbeek reached it independently in 1948. Unlike the earlier Levine–Dube theory, it explained how stability depends on the {{ref:soil-chem-202}} of the electrolyte. Yet other forces matter too, and it cannot describe colloidal crystals forming in dilute, low-salt dispersions.

soil-chem-161.title: Peptization: turning a precipitate back into a colloid
soil-chem-161.text: A settled precipitate can be coaxed back into suspension. Peptization does this by shaking the solid with a suitable electrolyte, a peptizing agent, until its particles form a {{ref:soil-chem-154}} again. It is the reverse of flocculation, also called deflocculation. Concentrated salt compresses the charged layer around each particle, which collapses in very salty solutions, so particles coalesce into an easily filtered precipitate. Wash it with too much deionized water and that layer re-expands, repulsion returns, and the precipitate peptizes. Freshly precipitated aluminium or iron hydroxide is very hard to filter, because its fine particles pass through paper.

soil-chem-167.title: Sepiolite, the fibrous clay of dry lands
soil-chem-167.text: Sepiolite is a soft, white, fibrous magnesium silicate clay, Mg4Si6O15(OH)2·6H2O, also known as meerschaum. It is one of the {{ref:soil-found-033}}. The fibrous clays form a continuous series from sepiolite, the richest in magnesium, to {{ref:soil-chem-110}}; sepiolite has the wider structural channels. It occurs as a secondary mineral with serpentine and can precipitate in arid environments. Soils of South Africa's arid west hold much of it, grading inland to palygorskite. It raises the water plants can use in sandy soils, but its cemented layers hamper mining. That cemented material is called sepiocrete.

soil-chem-150.title: Reading clay layers with X-rays
soil-chem-150.text: Clay minerals look nearly alike side to side. What sets them apart is height: the thickness of each stacked layer. Clay mineral X-ray diffraction measures that spacing. Ordered atoms diffract an X-ray beam at particular angles and intensities, from which the structure is calculated. Randomly oriented powders help little, because clays share similar X and Y dimensions. The diagnostic Z dimension is the height of the T-O or T-O-T layer described in {{ref:soil-chem-081}}, so samples are laid flat to strengthen basal (00l) reflections. The Z spacing shifts with cation substitution in the sheets and with the presence and size of the interlayer cation. Bragg's law, written l λ = 2d sin θ, gives the spacings, so successive 00l peaks are evenly spaced. Clays give broad peaks. Patterns are matched against known samples, such as the Clay Mineral Society's reference collection, because calculated patterns rarely fit. Harder nonclays such as quartz and feldspars are removed first by light crushing and sieving.

soil-chem-162.title: Hydrous oxides, porous metal compounds that grab other substances
soil-chem-162.text: Hydrous oxides are inorganic compounds of a metal, hydroxide and weakly bound water. Examples include hydrous ferric oxide (HFO), hydrous aluminium oxide (HAO), hydrous cupric oxide and hydrous titanium oxide. HFO and HAO precipitate in highly porous, poorly crystalline or amorphous forms. That open structure makes them good adsorbents, used for example in water treatment. They also form in nature. Oxidative {{ref:soil-found-058}} of rocks can produce HFO and HAO, giving clay soils rich in iron and aluminium hydrous oxides.

soil-chem-163.title: Iron oxides, the minerals that color and feed soils
soil-chem-163.text: Rust is the most familiar of a large family. Iron oxides are compounds of iron and oxygen, together with related ferric oxyhydroxides such as rust. They hold ferrous iron, ferric iron or both, and are often non-stoichiometric, with no fixed ratio of elements. Only a few matter at Earth's surface, chiefly wüstite, magnetite and {{ref:soil-chem-112}}. Among the oxyhydroxides, {{ref:soil-chem-104}} and {{ref:soil-chem-164}} are the commonest and the most important mineral carriers of iron in soils. Others include akaganéite, feroxyhyte, {{ref:soil-chem-111}} and {{ref:soil-chem-170}}. Iron(III) oxyhydroxide ranges from yellow through dark brown to black, depending on hydration, particle size and shape, and crystal structure. It precipitates from iron(III) solutions at pH 6.5 to 8 and forms readily when iron(II) hydroxide meets air. Some bacteria, such as Shewanella oneidensis and Geobacter species, even breathe on these minerals, handing them the electrons left over from their metabolism.

soil-chem-164.title: Lepidocrocite, the scaly red rust of wet places
soil-chem-164.text: Iron that rusts underwater forms lepidocrocite, an iron oxide-hydroxide, γ-FeO(OH), also called esmeraldite or hydrohematite. Red to reddish brown, it is common where primary iron minerals weather. Its layers of iron(III) oxide octahedra are held by hydrogen bonds through hydroxide layers, as in boehmite. These weak bonds give the mineral its scaly habit. In oxidizing conditions {{ref:soil-chem-170}} generally turns into lepidocrocite and {{ref:soil-chem-104}}. First described in 1813 from Moravia, it takes its name from the Greek for scale and fibre.

soil-chem-166.title: Maghemite, the magnetic mark of fire
soil-chem-166.text: A bushfire can leave its signature in the soil's magnetism. Maghemite, γ-Fe2O3, is a ferrimagnetic iron oxide with the formula of {{ref:soil-chem-112}} but the spinel structure of magnetite. It forms by weathering or low-temperature oxidation of iron(II) spinels such as magnetite, or as lepidocrocite and ferrihydrite lose water. It is a widespread brown or yellow pigment in sediments and soils. Heat converts goethite and ferrihydrite to maghemite and raises soil magnetism. Maghemite enrichment across a landscape therefore points to fire. A soil's magnetic susceptibility reflects magnetic iron oxides such as maghemite, and geoarchaeologists measure it.

soil-chem-165.title: Limonite, the iron ore that is really a mixture
soil-chem-165.text: Limonite was once thought to be a single mineral. It is now a field term for an iron ore made of a variable mixture of hydrated iron(III) oxide-hydroxides, including {{ref:soil-chem-104}}, lepidocrocite, akaganeite and jarosite. Only X-ray diffraction can settle its exact makeup. It forms by hydration of hematite and magnetite, oxidation of iron sulfides and weathering of iron-rich minerals, and is often the main iron component of lateritic soils. Its name comes from Greek words for a damp meadow or marshy lake, after its occurrence as bog iron ore. Its yellowish-brown streak tells it from hematite, with a red streak, and magnetite, with a black one.

soil-chem-168.title: Measuring surface area: the answer depends on the ruler
soil-chem-168.text: The surface area of a powder has no single true value. Measuring {{ref:soil-phys-043}}, the area per unit mass, is most often done by gas {{ref:soil-chem-145}} with the BET method. Results depend on the probe molecule's size, the exposed crystal faces and the temperature. The BET method captures fine structure and deep texture, but values can differ markedly with the gas used. Calculating area from particle sizes needs an assumed shape and misses surface texture. Gas permeability through a powder bed is quick and simple but misses much deep texture. Standards such as ISO 9277 govern the measurement.

soil-chem-153.title: Layer charge, the negative pull of clay sheets
soil-chem-153.text: Swap a silicon ion for an aluminium ion, and a clay layer gains a negative charge. Layer charge is the net negative charge created when ions of lower charge, such as Al3+, replace Si4+ through {{ref:soil-chem-085}}. Interlayer cations balance it. Where the charge sits defines minerals. In nontronite usually more than 60% lies in the tetrahedral sheet, generally balanced by Ca2+ or Mg2+, and {{ref:soil-chem-152}} is defined by more than 50% there. In the manganese oxide {{ref:soil-chem-195}}, cations and water between layers offset the charge, letting it exchange cations. The size of the balancing cation changes the layer spacing seen by X-ray diffraction.

soil-chem-152.title: Beidellite, a smectite charged in its silica sheet
soil-chem-152.text: Beidellite is a {{ref:soil-chem-091}} clay in which more than half the {{ref:soil-chem-153}} comes from aluminium replacing silicon in the tetrahedral sheet. It is a dioctahedral smectite, grouped with montmorillonite and nontronite, whereas saponite is trioctahedral. Beidellite is also one of the clays that make soils shrink and swell, along with smectite, montmorillonite, illite and vermiculite.

soil-chem-159.title: The Schulze–Hardy rule: why aluminium salts clump clay best
soil-chem-159.text: Doubling an ion's charge does far more than double its power to clump colloids. The Schulze–Hardy rule says the critical coagulation concentration of an electrolyte varies as the inverse sixth power of its counter-ion's charge. For trivalent counter-ions it falls to 0.03 to 0.5 × 10⁻³ mol/L. So multivalent cations flocculate colloids far better than monovalent ones: AlCl3 beats CaCl2, which beats NaCl. The rule can be derived from {{ref:soil-chem-157}}. Ions of the same charge still differ somewhat, reflecting particle properties or how strongly ions favor the surface.

soil-chem-149.title: Clay chemistry, from fertile fields to Mars
soil-chem-149.text: In 2009, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter spotted clay minerals on Mars, strong evidence that the planet once had water. Clay chemistry is the applied branch of chemistry that studies the structures, properties and reactions of clays and clay minerals. These minerals are built of nanometer-scale layers. They carry fixed and exchangeable charges, take molecules onto their surfaces and between their layers, and form stable colloidal dispersions. Their capacity to hold cations balances the commonest soil cations and controls pH, directly affecting how fertile a soil is. Their interactions with organic substances help fix nutrients and decide whether {{ref:soil-env-237}} and other contaminants are held or leached.

soil-chem-145.title: Adsorption, the art of sticking to a surface
soil-chem-145.text:
Every surface is a little unfinished. Atoms inside a solid are surrounded by neighbors, but those at the surface are not, and that leftover surface energy lets them attract other substances. The result is adsorption: the adhesion of atoms, ions or molecules from a gas, liquid or solution to a surface. It builds a film of adsorbate on the adsorbent. Unlike absorption, it does not penetrate into the bulk of the material. {{ref:soil-chem-068}} covers both, and {{ref:soil-chem-147}} is the reverse.

The bonds vary in strength. Physisorption works through weak van der Waals forces; chemisorption through covalent bonds. Electrostatic attraction can also hold adsorbates. The difference shows with water. Physically adsorbed water on a solid is removed by drying, while chemically adsorbed water may split into surface -H and -OH groups.

Adsorption, ion exchange and chromatography are all sorption processes. Each selectively moves substances from a fluid onto insoluble particles. In soil, the fluid is often the {{ref:soil-found-079}}. The German physicist Heinrich Kayser coined the word in 1881.

soil-chem-146.title: Adsorption isotherms: counting what a surface holds
soil-chem-146.text: How much will a surface hold if the supply keeps rising? An adsorption isotherm answers. It describes how much substance is adsorbed as a function of its pressure, or its concentration in solution, at constant temperature. The amount is nearly always divided by the adsorbent's mass, so materials can be compared. Freundlich and Kuster published the first isotherm, a purely empirical fit. Langmuir derived the first scientifically based one. His model assumes equivalent sites holding one molecule each, a uniform surface and at most a single layer, assumptions seldom all true. The 1938 BET isotherm allows multiple layers. Langmuir usually suits chemisorption, BET physisorption on surfaces without tiny pores. Choosing between Langmuir and Freundlich should rest on adsorption enthalpies, not best fit: constant in Langmuir's model, falling with coverage in Freundlich's. A Langmuir fit also yields the monolayer capacity, from which surface area can be calculated.

soil-chem-147.title: Desorption, letting go of a surface
soil-chem-147.text: Desorption is {{ref:soil-chem-145}} run backward: the release of adsorbed atoms or molecules from a surface into the surrounding fluid or vacuum. It happens when a molecule gains enough energy to overcome the barrier and binding energy holding it. Heat, light, energetic particle beams or reactions such as oxidation or reduction can supply it. The Polanyi–Wigner equation describes desorption driven by heat, linking surface coverage to desorption rate. The same idea cleans soil. As a cleanup method, {{ref:soil-env-230}} heats contaminated material to 90–560 °C, driving off water and organic contaminants for a gas treatment system to collect or destroy.

soil-chem-148.title: Chemical equivalents: counting charge, not just atoms
soil-chem-148.text: A millimole of calcium does twice the work of a millimole of sodium. The chemical equivalent captures this. It is the amount of a substance that reacts with, or supplies, one mole of hydrogen ions in an acid–base reaction. In a {{ref:soil-chem-113}} reaction, it is one mole of electrons. The number of equivalents of an ion equals its moles times its valence. So 1 mmol of Na+ is 1 milliequivalent, but 1 mmol of Ca2+ is 2 milliequivalents. The quantity is archaic, yet small amounts are still given in milliequivalents (meq), thousandths of an equivalent.
